# Always check existing ADRs; always write one when research finishes

## When to apply

Two distinct moments in any change that involves a decision:

- **Before starting** research, investigation, vendor evaluation, design
  exploration, refactor planning, or any non-obvious technical choice
- **After finishing** that work, and before merging the implementation PR

These are not optional. They are the load-bearing discipline that keeps a
codebase's intent recoverable. Skip them and the *why* of every decision
lives only in chat threads and senior engineers' heads — the exact failure
mode Doctyze exists to prevent.

## Step 1 — Before research: read the existing ADRs

Run this checklist before you start:

- [ ] List every ADR under `docs/architecture/decisions/` (`ls docs/architecture/decisions/`)
- [ ] Identify which existing ADRs touch the area you're about to explore
  (search the titles + the first paragraph of context)
- [ ] Read those ADRs fully — especially the **Alternatives rejected** section
- [ ] If a relevant ADR already exists and your research would supersede it,
  plan to write a *new* ADR that supersedes it (ADRs are append-only;
  never edit an accepted ADR)
- [ ] If your research would *reinforce* an existing ADR, you may still
  write a new ADR linking back — but do not duplicate the rationale

This step takes 10–20 minutes. It will repeatedly save you from re-litigating
decisions the team already made and abandoned.

## Step 2 — During research: keep a working notes file

Open `docs/investigations/YYYY-MM-DD-<slug>.md` and capture as you go:

- The question being answered
- The sources consulted (links, papers, vendor docs, internal Slack threads)
- The hypotheses considered
- The data / experiments / benchmarks
- The conclusions

These notes become the **Context** and **Alternatives** sections of the ADR
later. Without them, you'll reconstruct the reasoning from memory, badly.

## Step 3 — When research finishes: write the ADR

The instant the research produces a decision, write the ADR. Not later,
not "after the implementation lands" — in the same PR that introduces the
behavior the decision drives.

Use the MADR template (see [`write-adr`](write-adr.md) skill for full details):

```markdown
# ADR-NNNN — <title that names the decision, not the question>

- Status: accepted
- Date: YYYY-MM-DD
- Confidence: 🟢 CONFIRMED
- Supersedes: ADR-MMMM   (if applicable)

## Context
What situation forced this decision?

## Decision
What did we choose? Be specific.

## Alternatives rejected
At least 2–4 alternatives, with the reason each was rejected.
**This is the load-bearing section.** Future readers need to know not just
what we chose but what we considered and abandoned, and why.

## Consequences
Both positive and negative.

## Research sources
Link to the investigation notes file from Step 2.
Link to specific evidence (RFCs, vendor docs, benchmark results).
```

## Step 4 — Cross-link

Once the ADR is committed:

- Update the investigation notes file in `docs/investigations/` to link to
  the ADR
- If the decision affects a runbook or skill, update the affected
  canonical file in the same PR
- If the decision changes a documented pattern, update `AGENTS.md` so AI
  agents pick it up immediately

## Why this matters

Research that doesn't end in an ADR is wasted work. The team will face the
same decision again in 6 months, the same alternatives will be re-evaluated,
and the same conclusion will probably be reached — but at full cost,
twice. ADRs are how you pay the research cost *once*.

Equally: research that begins without checking existing ADRs duplicates
work that's already been done. Worse, it can produce a decision that
contradicts a prior decision the team is still operating under — which is
how systems silently become inconsistent.

## For AI coding agents

If you are an AI agent being asked to investigate, evaluate options, or
propose a design:

1. **First**, list ADRs under `docs/architecture/decisions/` and read any
   whose title touches the area you're investigating. Cite them in your
   response.
2. **Last**, if your investigation produces a recommendation, propose a
   new ADR file as part of your output. Do not just answer the question
   in chat; the answer belongs in the repository.
3. **Never** silently override an existing accepted ADR. If your
   recommendation contradicts a current ADR, explicitly state which one
   and that the new ADR will supersede it.

The Doctyze doc-guard GitHub Action will warn on PRs that introduce
behavior the existing ADRs describe without referencing or superseding
those ADRs.

## Anti-patterns

- **"It's just an investigation, no decision yet."** Then nothing about
  this rule applies *yet*. The moment a decision is made — including the
  decision *not* to change anything — that decision is an ADR.
- **"The decision is obvious."** Obvious decisions are exactly the ones
  most likely to be silently reversed by someone in 6 months who thinks
  the *other* choice is obvious. Write the ADR.
- **"I'll write the ADR after the implementation lands."** You won't.
  Either it goes in the same PR or it doesn't go in at all.
- **"There are too many existing ADRs to read."** Then the *first* ADR
  you should write is one that proposes an index / categorization
  scheme. Discovery is a real problem, but skipping the read step is
  not the fix.
